ethical-hacking-and-authorization.title: Welcome to Ethical hacking, authorization and the law, part of Ethical Hacking.
ethical-hacking-and-authorization.idea: Every technique in this course is dual-use. The same scan that finds an exposed database for a client, pointed at a system you do not own, is a criminal act in most jurisdictions — including Ghana, where the Cybersecurity Act 2020 (Act 1038) provides for offences relating to unauthorised access to computer systems. Professional practice is therefore not a set of politeness rules; it is the structure that makes the work legal, insurable and useful.
ethical-hacking-and-authorization.example: An engagement letter covers app.client.example and its staging environment. During reconnaissance you find a shared hosting provider, and the staging domain resolves to the same IP range as admin.client.example, a system not mentioned in the scope. What do you do? The professional answer has four steps and no improvisation. First, stop: do not scan, do not click, do not "just check one thing". Second, document: note the observation, the time and the evidence that led to it (a DNS record, publicly available). Third, ask: message the engagement contact in writing, describing what you found and proposing to add the system to scope with a written amendment. Fourth, continue only with in-scope work while you wait. If the client agrees, the amendment records the new host, the technique limits and the time window. If they do not, the finding still goes in the report as an observation about infrastructure that appears related but was not tested — which is itself useful information for them. The counterfactual is instructive: a tester who scans the extra host "because it is obviously theirs" has, in the eyes of the law, accessed a computer system without authorisation. The engagement being friendly does not change that, and neither does the fact that nothing was damaged.
ethical-hacking-and-authorization.challenge: Prepare a complete engagement pack for a fictional client: a scope table, rules of engagement, a prohibition list, escalation contacts, a data-handling note, and a report template. Then have somebody play the client and try to get you to test an out-of-scope system before signing an amendment — and write down, in one paragraph, exactly what you said.

reconnaissance-and-surface-mapping.title: Welcome to Reconnaissance and mapping the attack surface, part of Ethical Hacking.
reconnaissance-and-surface-mapping.idea: An attacker's advantage is patience: they can spend a week learning about a target with tools that are entirely legal, because reading public information is not an intrusion. A defender's counter-advantage is that the same information tells them what they have left exposed. Reconnaissance is therefore the phase that most repays practice, and the one that most beginners skip.
reconnaissance-and-surface-mapping.example: The authorised scope is one domain and its subdomains. The passive phase produces a list before any scan is run; the active phase (permitted, in hours, at low intensity) adds the technical detail. The output is deliberately boring and structured: a host table, a service list with versions, a web surface list, and an observation section for things that are interesting but unconfirmed. Note how much of the report's future value comes from writing it down as you go — the difference between a productive second day and a lost one is the notes from the first. Two discipline points. First, tag every item with how it was found (passive source, scan, manual browsing), because the report needs to distinguish "publicly visible" from "we probed it". Second, resist exploiting anything yet: the reconnaissance phase ends when you can describe the surface, and exploitation begins with a hypothesis worth proving, not with curiosity.
reconnaissance-and-surface-mapping.challenge: Produce a complete attack-surface map for a system you own or have written permission to assess: hosts and IP ranges with how each was discovered, services and versions, web endpoints and parameters, cloud storage references, and a ranked list of the five items most likely to be exploitable. Do not exploit anything. Then write the two recommendations you would put first in a report, based only on the map.

web-and-system-exploitation.title: Welcome to Exploitation: how weaknesses become access, part of Ethical Hacking.
web-and-system-exploitation.idea: Exploitation is the phase learners wait for, and the one that most often produces a false sense of skill. The techniques are not the difficulty; the discipline is. A professional test proves impact with the smallest possible action, captures evidence, then stops — and spends the rest of the time on the systemic reasons the weakness existed, because the same code will be written again next sprint.
web-and-system-exploitation.example: An authenticated user of an invoice application changes an identifier in a request. The response contains another customer's invoice, including their name, address and amount owed. That is broken access control, and it is a serious finding. The professional sequence from here is short and disciplined. First, demonstrate with one identifier beyond the user's own account, using an account the client provisioned for testing — not by walking through a hundred invoices. Second, capture the request and response with the sensitive fields redacted in the report but visible in the evidence attached to the ticket. Third, verify the impact claim by answering the questions a compliance officer will ask: does this disclose personal data (yes — which makes it a reportable data-protection matter in many jurisdictions); can it be used to modify, not just read (test once, carefully, if scope allows); does it affect every customer or a subset? Fourth, stop, and escalate immediately rather than continuing to map the extent, because the extent is now the client's incident, not your exploration. Then the part that makes the finding useful: the systemic cause. The endpoint builds its query from a client-supplied identifier with no ownership check, and the same pattern appears in four other files. The remediation is therefore not "patch line 42" but "enforce ownership in the data-access layer", plus a test that fails if a new endpoint is added without it. Report severity using CVSS for consistency, but pair it with plain language about consequence — a rating of 7.5 means little to a director; "any logged-in user can read any customer's invoice" means everything.
web-and-system-exploitation.challenge: Complete one full assessment of a lab application or a system you own: a testing checklist from the OWASP WSTG, at least three findings of different classes with full reproductions, one business-logic finding, and for each a systemic root cause and a remediation with a proposed regression test. Redact all personal data, and stop at the smallest proof of impact for every issue.

reporting-defences-and-career.title: Welcome to Reporting, defence and the security career, part of Ethical Hacking.
reporting-defences-and-career.idea: Clients do not buy vulnerabilities; they buy a reduced chance of being breached, and the report is the only instrument that delivers it. This lesson closes the course by turning findings into change, and by being explicit about the professional and legal obligations that continue after the engagement ends — including what to do when you find a serious bug in a system nobody asked you to test.
reporting-defences-and-career.example: A two-week engagement produced 31 findings. The client's board will read one page. Compare two versions of that page. Version A (technical): a list of the top findings with their CVSS vectors and a sentence each about the mechanics. Accurate, and hard for a director to act on: every item looks equally urgent, none is tied to a consequence, and the reader cannot tell what happens next. Version B: three sentences of context, three named risks with consequences, and three decisions with owners and dates. It contains no vulnerability names at all in the first paragraph, and it is still technically honest — the detail lives in the sections that follow. The difference is not dumbing down; it is translating. The board does not need to know what an unsafe object reference is. It needs to know that customer invoices are readable by any logged-in user, that this is a personal-data exposure with a legal dimension, that fixing the pattern properly takes an estimated three days of a developer's time, and that a temporary control (restricting the affected endpoint to internal users) can be in place today. Version B is what converts findings into a budget line, an owner and a date — which is the only outcome that reduces risk.
reporting-defences-and-career.challenge: Produce a complete, client-ready penetration test report for a lab environment or a system you own with written self-authorization: executive summary, scope and methodology, at least five ranked findings with reproductions and redacted evidence, a remediation plan with effort estimates, and a re-test plan. Then implement two of the fixes, re-run the original reproductions, and append the verification results — including anything that did not work the first time.
